title: The Cartoon of the Grieving Widow
scenario: Cartoonist Benedikt Aigner at a Salzburg daily draws a sharp cartoon mocking a politician who exploited a disaster for photo-ops, using the image of a widowed flood victim next to him. A local woman recognises herself and says the drawing turns her real grief into a joke. The cartoon has been widely shared, and the political point has resonated. His editor says satire needs targets, and the widow was not the target. Benedikt could withdraw the cartoon, redraw it, or stand by it. The politician's lawyers are watching.
options: Stand by the cartoon unchanged, explaining that the target was the politician and the widow's image served the critique.
Redraw it with a generic figure instead of her likeness and publicly apologise to her for the distress.
Withdraw it altogether and draw a new satire of the politician that does not involve any real victim.
tension: satirical licence vs. harm to a victim

title: Mocking the Prophet's Followers
scenario: Comedian and late-night host Karim Bensalem in Tunis plans a sketch lampooning a hardline preacher, who is notorious for inciting hatred, by exaggerating his sermons. His writers warn the sketch may be read as ridiculing ordinary worshippers, who are sensitive about religion, and some of their families have already faced harassment. The station's lawyer fears riots, not lawsuits. Karim believes laughing at the powerful matters, especially after threats to journalists. Recording is tomorrow and the network wants a decision tonight.
options: Record the sketch as written, trusting that viewers can distinguish the preacher from ordinary believers.
Rewrite the sketch to target only the preacher's own known statements, removing any imitation of ritual or worship.
Shelve the sketch for now, and wait for tensions to cool before returning to the preacher.
tension: free expression vs. risk of violence

title: Satire After the Mine Collapse
scenario: Producer Sibusiso Dube of a Bulawayo satirical radio show is preparing an episode mocking a mining company chief who dismissed safety concerns days before a collapse killed eleven workers. The writers' draft includes a jingle with the dead miners' voices re-enacted. The widows' association has asked comedians to stay away. The company chief's remarks were callous, and the show has a loyal audience that looks to it for catharsis. Sibusiso must finalise the episode and decide how to balance anger and respect.
options: Air the episode with the jingle removed, aiming the satire solely at the chief's remarks and corporate culture.
Air it as written, believing that anger at the company belongs in satire even when the subject is painful.
Postpone the episode by a month and consult the widows' association before deciding on content.
tension: catharsis vs. respect for the bereaved

title: The Meme of the Opposition Leader
scenario: Social media manager Dalila Haxhiu at a Tirana satirical page creates a meme showing a female opposition leader's face edited onto an animal, to mock her policy flip-flop. The meme gets massive engagement, but replies fill with misogynistic abuse, and the leader's daughters are mentioned. Dalila did not intend that. Her page has a mixed audience of students and professionals. Removing the meme might be seen as bowing to pressure. Keeping it may drive more abuse. She has to decide whether to delete, pin a statement, or let it run.
options: Keep the meme and moderate the replies harshly, removing abusive comments and blocking repeat offenders.
Delete the meme and post a note acknowledging that the image invited the wrong kind of response.
Replace the meme with a new one that mocks only the policy flip-flop, using her words and not her body.

title: The Parody Account Mistaken for News
scenario: Founder Chidera Nwosu of a Port Harcourt parody news site writes a fake story claiming the governor will ban motorbike taxis, in the style of a straight report. It is meant to ridicule the governor's rumoured plans. Overnight the story is believed and shared widely; riders, who depend on income, are in uproar and some have blocked roads. The site carries a small disclaimer at the footer. Chidera has to decide whether to delete the story, put a banner on it, or leave it as a satire.
options: Delete the story and post a clear explanation that it was satire, apologising to riders who were misled.
Leave the story but add a large banner saying it is satire and pin a statement on social channels.
Leave it as is, since the satirical nature is established and the governor's rumoured plans are a fair target.

title: Mocking a Disabled Candidate's Debate Performance
scenario: Writer Hiroshi Tanabe on a Tokyo comedy panel show prepares a joke about a candidate whose speech was halting during a debate. The writers know the candidate has a speech impairment, which he has spoken about openly. They also know his policies are controversial and he has a history of mocking others. Hiroshi believes the joke is aimed at the candidate's evasiveness rather than his impairment, but he can see how viewers with similar conditions would hear it. The jokes are due to the director in an hour.
options: Cut the joke and write one about the candidate's policy evasions, leaving his speech out of it altogether.
Keep the joke as written, since a public figure's debate performance is open to comment and the target is evasiveness.
Keep a version of the joke that explicitly separates his impairment from his evasiveness, so the distinction is clear.

title: Deadpan Piece on Refugee Quotas
scenario: Columnist Odalys Ruiz at a Miami weekly writes a deadpan satirical column proposing absurd quotas for human arrivals, mimicking arguments used by restrictionist politicians. A lawyer friend warns that the piece reads as sincere to some, and that extremist forums have already quoted similar satire as serious support. Odalys's aim is to expose the cruelty of the policy rhetoric. Her editor loves the piece. Refugee advocates are split on whether it helps. She must decide whether to run it as is, add a note, or rewrite.
options: Run the column unchanged, trusting readers and preserving the sharpness of the satire.
Run it with a short editor's note identifying it as satire, accepting that this dulls the effect.
Rewrite it as an open polemic that states her objections directly, abandoning the deadpan form.
tension: satire's ambiguity vs. risk of endorsement

title: The Puppet and the Prime Minister's Illness
scenario: Puppet-show producer Emeka Eze, whose popular political satire airs on Lagos television, is writing an episode where the prime minister puppet falls asleep in meetings. Real reports say the head of government is battling a serious illness and has been absent from many functions. The writers' joke is against absentee governance, but it could read as mocking illness. The prime minister's staff deny any illness. A senior writer says leaders with unknowns about health deserve questions. Emeka has to approve the script for recording.
options: Approve the sleeping-in-meetings gag, framed around absent leadership and denial by staff rather than illness.
Cut the gag entirely until medical facts are known, to avoid mocking a person who may be genuinely ill.
Replace it with a joke about the staff's refusal to answer questions, which still pursues the transparency issue.
tension: accountability of leaders vs. mocking illness

title: A Satirical Obituary for a Dead Dictator
scenario: Obituaries editor Teodora Marinescu in Bucharest drafts a satirical obituary of a dictator-era official who died free of prosecution. The piece lists his crimes in mock-flattering language. His family asks that the paper hold off during the funeral week. Survivors of the regime's prison network applaud the draft, which they feel gives them the justice denied. The paper's old readers respect the dead; younger readers want honesty. Teodora must decide whether to run it now, delay it, or turn it into a straight piece.
options: Run the satirical obituary now, as the public deserves an account while the death is in the news.
Delay the satirical piece for a few weeks, out of respect to the funeral week, while running a factual obituary.
Run only a straight obituary that lists his documented crimes plainly, without mock-flattering language.
tension: historical justice vs. respect for mourning

title: Teenager's Prank Video With a Politician
scenario: Youth channel producer Lerato Phiri in Maseru edits a prank video in which a teen host pranks a minister's driver by pretending the minister has been kidnapped. The driver panicked for several minutes and later fainted. The team intended to mock the minister's heavy security, but the driver, a poor man, is a victim. The footage is hilarious and likely to go viral. Lerato's channel is struggling and needs a hit. The driver has reportedly not agreed to broadcast the clip. She has a deadline tonight.
options: Do not release the video, and apologise to the driver, offering him compensation for the distress.
Release the video only after getting the driver's explicit, informed consent and paying him a fee.
Release a modified version in which the driver is obscured, since the satire concerns the minister's security.
tension: viral success vs. harm to a bystander

title: The Billboard Satire
scenario: Street-art collective organiser Sunita Joshi in Pune plans a billboard parody of a utility company's ad: smiling families under 'We Light Your Life', altered to show candles and the slogan 'We Light Your Wait'. Power cuts have hit hospitals and small shops, and the satire could hearten the public. The company's lawyers might sue for trademark misuse, and the billboard owner might lose his lease. A volunteer fears the joke trivialises people who suffered a death on a ventilator during a cut. Sunita must decide before the installation crew arrives.
options: Install the parody billboard as designed, accepting legal risk and the volunteer's concerns about tone.
Change the slogan to target the company's failure to maintain the grid without reference to hospitals.
Cancel the billboard and instead hold a public meeting where affected families can speak about the outages.
tension: public anger vs. sensitivity to loss

title: Impersonating a Pastor for a Laugh
scenario: Comedian Winston Baptiste on a Port of Spain morning show performs a character imitating a well-known televangelist, who is accused of financial wrongdoing, using his exact catchphrases. The televangelist's congregation includes many elderly, devout viewers who find it hurtful. Winston has support from colleagues who regard the televangelist as a fraud. The station's manager is uneasy about losing older viewers and sponsors. Winston must decide whether to continue the character in the show's next episodes, soften it, or drop it.
options: Keep the character as it is, since the televangelist is a public figure accused of exploiting believers.
Tone down the imitation of devotional practices and focus on the money allegations rather than sincere worship.
Drop the character and cover the allegations in a straight segment with a guest financial expert.
tension: mocking a powerful figure vs. hurting believers

title: A Joke About a Vanished Person
scenario: Writer Mirela Dedić at a Sarajevo satirical weekly prepares a piece mocking a missing-persons commission for incompetence, including a gag about 'finding people faster by not looking'. A reader group of families whose relatives vanished in the war complains that the humour dismisses their decades of pain. The commission's failures are well documented, and the piece may pressure it into action. Her editor sees the gag as the sharpest line. Mirela feels the weight of both the criticism and the cause and has to decide on the final text.
options: Keep the gag, since its target is the commission's institutional failure, and print a note that families were not the intended target.
Cut the gag and write the satire around budgets and bureaucratic delays, avoiding any joke about the missing.
Show the draft to a representative of the families before publication, and adjust according to the response.

title: Comic Strip About a Local Landlord
scenario: Cartoonist Fatuma Warsame in Mombasa draws a weekly strip for a community paper. She wants to mock a landlord who evicts tenants at short notice by portraying him as a greedy crab. He is an easily identified local figure, and the crab's shell bears the name of his building. The landlord has hired thugs before. Tenants love the idea. The paper's lawyer says the risk is defamation and physical danger. Fatuma could name him, blur identifying details, or switch to a general figure. Her deadline is today.
options: Publish it with the building's name and clear likeness, as the tenants and public interest justify direct satire.
Publish a version with a generic 'Landlord Crab' and no identifying marks, shielding herself and the paper.
Delay the strip while she consults the tenants' association and a lawyer about safe ways to name him.
tension: satire as accountability vs. personal safety

title: Satire and the Election Rumour
scenario: Satire editor Henrietta Voss at a Melbourne site writes a fake news story saying a party leader will resign because of ill health. In an election week, the story, though labelled, gets screenshotted without the label and circulates in group chats. A radio host reads it out. The party demands removal. Henrietta thinks removal will make the site seem to bow to pressure, but the screenshots are already beyond control. She wonders whether the joke's absurdity should have protected it and what responsibility she holds for stripped labels.
options: Remove the story and publish a note explaining why, accepting a responsibility to avoid election-week confusion.
Leave the story up with its label intact and issue a statement that screenshots stripped of context are beyond her control.
Keep it up but pin a clarification at the top and contact the radio host to correct the broadcast.
tension: responsibility for downstream use vs. freedom to joke

title: The Satirist's Anonymous Sources
scenario: Anonymous blogger and satirist known as 'The Quill' in Minsk is contacted by a mid-level official who feeds him true insider details to be turned into jokes about the regime. Exact details in the satire might expose the official. The blogger wants to preserve the comedic sharpness, while knowing that real details make the humour land. Over time he realises the official craves a cause. The blogger must decide whether to continue using precise details, to blur them, or to end the relationship.
options: Continue using precise details, but only those that dozens of officials could plausibly know.
Replace real details with invented composites, keeping the humour but removing the risk to the official.
End the relationship and tell the official to seek a protected whistleblower route instead.
tension: using a source as a tool vs. caring for them

title: Mocking a Grieving Football Fan Base
scenario: Sports comedian Gaël Dupuis in Marseille prepares a segment mocking a rival club's fans after a stadium crush in which people died. Dupuis's targets are the club's chairman who ignored safety warnings, but the segment's shock opening uses fans' chants. The family of one victim writes asking him to cancel. The comedian's followers dislike the rival club and are eager. His producer says the segment can be edited to address the chairman only. Gaël has until the evening to submit the edit.
options: Submit the version that targets only the chairman's negligence, with no chants or references to fans.
Submit the original, reasoning that sports fans accept rival banter and the target is blameworthy.
Cancel the segment and visit the victim's family to hear their concerns before deciding on any future treatment.

title: Fake Press Release Prank
scenario: Activist-journalist Joaquim Fernandes in Lisbon sends a fake press release in the name of an oil company announcing it will stop drilling, to mock its green claims and publicise its practices. Several outlets pick it up before it is debunked, and the company's shares drop briefly. Joaquim's collective says the prank exposes the gap between rhetoric and action. The company says investors lost money, and journalists feel deceived. Joaquim must decide how to respond to the backlash and whether to confess authorship.
options: Confess authorship publicly, explain the aim, and accept consequences, treating the hoax as a deliberate act of satire.
Stay silent and let the debunking run its course, since confessing could bring legal action on his collective.
Publish a detailed account of the company's actual practices, framed as the reason for the hoax, without claiming authorship.
tension: satirical hoax vs. deception of journalists and investors

title: The Satire That Targets a Whole Region
scenario: Sketch writer Mikael Johansson in Gothenburg drafts a skit about a northern rural town, depicting residents as slow and backward, a common stereotype in Swedish comedy. A writer from that region argues it reinforces prejudice that makes rural youth leave and discourages investment. Others say the humour is affectionate and the town in question has embraced earlier jokes. The skit is funny and has been audience-tested. Mikael must decide whether to keep, reshape or cut it, as the show tapes this week.
options: Keep the skit, since regional stereotypes are a long-established comic tradition and affection mitigates the sting.
Rework it so that the humour comes from the characters' wit rather than backwardness, reversing the stereotype.
Cut the skit and replace it with one that satirises urban metropolitan snobbery instead.
tension: affectionate humour vs. impact on communities

title: Spoof Ad About a Public Health Campaign
scenario: Creative director Noor Al-Mansour at a Doha satire studio makes a spoof of a government anti-smoking campaign that exaggerates its gory images. The humour targets the campaign's clumsy tone. However, a health researcher warns that undermining a campaign that works may deter vulnerable young people from quitting. The studio's audience includes many teenagers. The campaign's own agency responds with irritation. Noor has the finished video and must choose between releasing it, adding a disclaimer, or reworking it.
options: Release the spoof as is, trusting that audiences can enjoy the joke without changing their health behaviour.
Release it with a closing message affirming the importance of quitting and linking to support services.
Rework the spoof to target the clumsy bureaucracy of the campaign's slogans rather than its health messages.

title: A Cartoon Banned by the Editor
scenario: Staff cartoonist Gabriela Salazar in Quito submits a cartoon depicting the president as a puppet of a foreign lender. The editor, Armando Pinto, refuses to print it, saying the image echoes antisemitic tropes about puppet-masters, which Gabriela did not intend. She says the lender is a bank, not a people, and the visual convention is common in political cartoons. Armando's view is shared by one board member. The paper's readers include a small Jewish community that has been vocal. Gabriela can accept, appeal to the publisher, or publish elsewhere.
options: Accept the decision and redraw the cartoon with a different visual metaphor for debt, such as a chain or leash.
Appeal to the publisher, arguing that the cartoon targets a bank and that the convention is not inherently antisemitic.
Publish the original on her personal page with an explanation, while accepting the editor's decision for the paper.
tension: intent vs. historical resonance of imagery

title: Parody Quotes From a Dead Poet
scenario: Satirical site editor Anjali Menon in Kochi invents quotes from a revered, deceased poet to criticise a current policy, writing them in the poet's style with a label noting they are fictional. Some schools quote the satire as authentic, and the poet's grandchildren are upset by attribution of views he never held. Anjali's team feels the satire has helped to challenge a bad policy. She is wondering whether to keep the quotes, retract them, or change the poet for a fictional character.
options: Keep the quotes with a more visible fictional label, and contact the grandchildren to explain the intention.
Retract the quotes and replace the poet with an invented character, to avoid misattributing views to a real person.
Keep the quotes and make no change, treating the label as sufficient and the misuse by schools as their error.
tension: respect for the dead vs. political critique

title: A Mock Trial of the Mayor
scenario: Community theatre journalist Aroha Ngata in Hamilton organises a live mock trial of the city mayor, with actors reading real quotes from council meetings, to satirise the mayor's refusal to hold public hearings. The mayor's staff claim that the event is a smear and that actors will distort the facts. A local councillor offers a real defence lawyer for balance. Audience members include people harmed by council decisions. Aroha wants it to be funny and fair and has to decide how to structure the script a week before the show.
options: Use only verbatim quotes with citations in the programme, and keep the satire in the staging and the commentary.
Invite the mayor to appear or send a representative, with equal time, and accept that the show may be less sharp.
Make the mock trial openly fictional, using a thinly disguised mayor figure to avoid disputes about accuracy.

title: The Satire That Became a Rallying Cry
scenario: Writer Tobias Brandt on a Zurich satire programme coins a mocking nickname for a populist politician, who loves it and adopts it as a brand. Supporters wear it on badges and chant it at rallies, some adding hostile slogans against minorities. Tobias feels his joke has been captured and now serves the politician's cause. His colleagues suggest retiring the nickname; others say the satire's meaning remains. He faces a choice about whether to keep using the nickname on air, which brings viewers.
options: Retire the nickname on air and say why, since it is now serving the politician's rallies.
Continue using the nickname, changing its context with new jokes that undercut the politician's embrace of it.
Keep using it unchanged, since the nickname's use by others is not the satirist's responsibility.
tension: responsibility for appropriated satire vs. continuity

title: Spoofing a Missing Child Alert
scenario: Radio comedian Zeynep Arslan in Izmir wants to spoof emergency alert sounds in a sketch about phone notifications, with a siren and a fake alert about a missing child. A listener recalls how a real alert brought her family relief after a real child was found. Zeynep's producer says the sketch is about pushy notifications, not about children. Parents' groups, however, warn that such parodies teach audiences to ignore real alerts. The sketch is funny and complete. Zeynep must decide whether it airs.
options: Air the sketch with the alert replaced by a made-up notification about something trivial, keeping the joke on pushy phones.
Air it as written, trusting that listeners understand the joke and do not confuse it with actual alerts.
Cut the sketch from the show, given that the alert system's credibility relies on public trust.
tension: comic creativity vs. public safety systems
